results.question: Team ES2005 had a per-unit production cost target from the start of the project. In the final meeting, what did the prototype first come to, what was the target, and how did they get back under budget?
results.gold_answer: The target was 12.50 Euros per unit (half the 25 Euro selling price). In the final meeting the Project Manager (C) said the prototype would cost 14.6 Euros; he suggested flattening the shape, and the Industrial Designer (A) noticed the double-curved case had been entered twice in the cost sheet. Taking out the duplicate brought it to 11.60 Euros, under the 12.50 limit.
results.answer: In the final meeting (ES2005d), Speaker C (Project Manager) reported the prototype's unit cost first came to 14.60 EUR, above the 12.50 EUR production cost target. They got back under budget by removing three costed items, including a duplicate double-curve on the casing, which brought the cost to 11.60 EUR. Flattening the shape was considered but was noted as saving less than hoped.

results.question: In ES2005's second meeting the Industrial Designer assumed the remote would run on ordinary batteries. What energy source did the team end up with, which alternatives were rejected, and who argued for the final choice?
results.gold_answer: In meeting b the Industrial Designer (A) suggested just regular batteries. results.answer: ES2005's team chose a rechargeable battery recharged on a base station that doubles as a stand, rather than the regular batteries Arlo (Industrial Designer) had assumed in meeting 2. Speaker B (Marketing Expert, Raj) argued for the rechargeable battery in meeting ES2005c, and Speaker C (Project Manager) backed him.

results.question: In team TS3005's functional design meeting, who argued for an LCD touch screen and with what evidence, who warned it clashed with keeping the remote cheap, and did the LCD survive the final costing?
results.gold_answer: The Marketing Expert (Speaker D) pushed for the LCD, citing survey figures: 81% of 16-25 year olds were interested in an LCD screen, and the target group was 16-45. The Industrial Designer (Speaker C) warned that LCD screens are very expensive and clash with the mission to make it cheap. The PM settled on 'for now it's LCD', with buttons as a backup. Speaker C (Industrial Designer) warned that this "collides with our mission to make it very cheap" because LCD and touch screens are expensive. The LCD survived the final costing in TS3005d: when the team checked the cost against the 12.50 EUR limit, they cut speech recognition, the microphone, the speaker and the scroll wheel instead, and Speaker D said the LCD could not be removed because "otherwise we don't have an L_C_D_ screen."

results.question: In team TS3008's conceptual design meeting, who pushed for an LCD display on the remote and how was it settled? In the final meeting, what did the component information say a display would need, and which chip did the team choose?
results.gold_answer: The Industrial Designer (Speaker C) pushed for an LCD (programme info, a trendy colour LCD). The PM (Speaker A) opposed it because it did not fit the sturdy, simple design and the docking station was already the special feature; D raised cost and fragility and B called it too much. A concluded 'we skip the LCD display'. In the final meeting the component information said a display requires an advanced chip, so with no display the team chose the simple chip.
results.answer: In TS3008c, Speaker C (Industrial Designer) pushed for an LCD on the remote, suggesting a TV guide or programme information, while Speaker A (Project Manager) argued it was vulnerable and didn't fit the sturdy, simple concept; the team skipped the LCD, with the decision recorded as settled against it after A invoked a veto and B and D agreed. In the final meeting, TS3008d, the component list said a display requires an advanced chip (Speaker B, User Interface Designer), and the team chose the simple chip, since a push-button needs only a simple chip and the display was dropped.

results.question: Team TS3008 adopted a base/docking station in its functional design meeting. Who proposed it and what was it for, and what happened to it in the final costing meeting?
results.gold_answer: In meeting b the Marketing Expert (Speaker D) proposed a base with a button that makes a lost remote beep (about 50% of users often lose their remote), and the PM (A) added making it rechargeable; in meeting c the PM called the docking station 'our killer feature'. In the final costing the docking station was not on the cost sheet. With one battery and a simple chip about 2.30 Euro of the 12.50 budget was left. D and B argued a docking station could be built for that, but the PM thought it unrealistic and suggested forgetting it (pushing kinetic power instead, which was not adopted), so the final concept had no docking station.
results.answer: In the second functional design meeting (TS3008b), Speaker A (Project Manager) proposed a rechargeable base, comparing it to mouse docks, so the remote would never need batteries and could always be found; Speaker D (Marketing Expert) added a button on the base to make the lost remote beep. It was only tentatively accepted, tied to the 12.50 EUR production cost. In the detailed design/costing meeting (TS3008d) it did not survive as planned: the cost sheet had no docking station line, A judged it would cost about a fifth of the remote's price, and it was left open, with kinetic power floated as a compromise.
